chapter_theme: The herdsman's work made into yoga. The flute songs end by penning the senses: dogs let loose cannot guard, the demon-mind must subside like a snake before the charmer's pipe, and 'I' and 'mine' must go. The milking songs then draw the nectar that tradition places in the head, above the palate, in the skull's egg, so that the body does not die, burn or stink and Yama is turned back. The herding songs pen the cattle of Saiva Siddhanta one by one, the two deeds, the three egoities, the souls of one, two and three malas, the three bodies, the three karmas, and leave the herdsman to see the great light in the crown and sit in silent nishta.
structure_note: 1832 to 1839 close the flute songs (புல்லாங்குழலூதல்), each stanza a two-line lesson with the refrain ஊதுகுழல் கோனே; 1840 to 1845 are the milking songs (பால் கறத்தல்), four claims per stanza about the milk; 1846 to 1856 open the herding songs (கிடை கட்டுதல்), in which each stanza names a herd of cattle to be penned, usually a numbered set from Siddhanta, and the section runs on into chapter 96. The refrains carry the form; the readings are what each stanza adds.

1832.reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, saying that those who have let the senses loose in every direction like dogs are demons.
1832.nuance: பேயர், demons or madmen, is strong: the unrestrained are not merely unwise but not human. The dogs return in 1835 and 1836, where the sense is worked out: an unleashed dog cannot guard.

1833.reading: Blow the flute with a rebuke, herdsman, so that those who run and roam about come to awareness.
1833.nuance: ஓடித் திரிவோர் may be the pilgrims and wanderers the Siddhars mock, or the straying mind of the next stanzas; சாடியே makes the flute's call a scolding. உணர்வு, awareness, is the recovery of attention, not new doctrine.

1834.reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, driving off the tigers that close in on the flocks of goats.
1834.nuance: The plainest herding line in the sequence, and the one most open. Tradition reads the flocks as the souls or the senses and the tigers as desire, disease or death; the verse itself gives only the shepherd's scene, and the Saiva pun on பசு (cow and bound soul) lies behind the whole section rather than in this word.

1835.reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, having tied up the Maricha dogs of dull nature.
1835.nuance: மாரீசம் is the name of the demon who deceived as a golden deer, so the dogs are the senses as deceivers, dull (மட்டி) in nature yet able to mislead; they are to be tied, not killed.

1836.reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, saying that dogs that are never tied are never fit for guarding.
1836.nuance: The argument of 1832 completed: restraint is what makes the senses useful. The claim is not that the senses are evil but that unleashed they cannot do the one thing a dog is for.

1837.reading: Blow the flute close, herdsman, so that the demon-mind subsides like a snake in its box.
1837.nuance: Here the flute is the snake-charmer's pipe, which makes the snake sway and settle back into the basket, so the image is literal for once: the mind is charmed down, not forced. The snake in the box is also the coiled power of Siddhar cipher, and the verse admits that reading too, as the Sivavakkiyam does at 1464.

1838.reading: Blow the flute as the Lord's own, herdsman, so that there is neither 'mine' nor 'I'.
1838.nuance: தனதாக, 'as his own', is read as the flute played as the Lord's and not the player's; the two words that go, எனது and யான், are the Kural's pair at 346. The sense of ownership is dissolved by handing the act itself over.

1839.reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, saying that what is learned is only this: the one place where all has fallen away, and the joining of what has fallen away with what is reached there.
1839.nuance: அற்ற இடம் ஒன்றே, the one place where things have ceased, is read as the void or the stilled mind; அற்றதோடு உற்றதைக் கற்றது is a play on three rhyming participles that I can only paraphrase. The verse sets a learning that is the end of learning against ordinary study.

1840.reading: Milk so as to remain without dying, the milk that is in the head; milk so as to remain without burning; milk within the bare open space.
1840.nuance: The milking songs (1840 to 1845) are cipher: பால், milk, is the nectar that tradition says the yogi draws from the moon in the head (சிரம்) once the breath is raised, and the deathless, unburning body is its fruit. Plainly they are a cowherd's work-song, and the poet keeps that surface throughout. வெட்டவெளி, the open space, is the place of the milking in both readings.

1841.reading: Milk the milk that stays untainted; milk so that old karma ends; milk the milk that is spat from the mouth; milk so as to eat it with an empty belly filled.
1841.nuance: வாயால் உமிழ்ந்திடும் பால், the milk the mouth spits out, is the stanza's riddle; tradition reads it as the nectar that drips from the palate when the tongue is turned back (கேசரி), swallowed rather than spat. வயிறார உண்டிட is the yogi who no longer needs food, and the plain sense is simply a full meal.

1842.reading: Milk the milk that does not go bad; milk so as to live on day after day; milk the milk that flows without ceasing; milk the milk that grows in the skull.
1842.nuance: தலை மண்டை, the skull, names the source directly; the three qualities (not stinking, unceasing, giving long life) are the tradition's claims for the inner nectar against the body's milk, which sours.

1843.reading: Milk the milk by which the world is loathed, the milk that is sheer retching; milk so that it falls into the pot; milk so that the full milk falls within the throat.
1843.nuance: ஒக்காளம், vomit, repeats 1817's disgust; here it is either the milk that makes the world nauseous to the drinker, or a milk that is itself a retching, which would make the stanza about the nectar rising rather than falling. கலசம், the pot, and கண்டம், the throat, place the milk in the body.

1844.reading: Milk without belching; milk so as to turn away Yama when he comes; milk so that the spark of fire goes to rest; milk so as to join supreme Siva.
1844.nuance: ஏப்பம், belching, is the sign of ordinary digestion that the nectar is said to be free of. தீப்பொறி ஓய்ந்திட is unclear: the body's heat, the fire of desire or the kindled fire of the breath, which the tradition says is cooled by the nectar; all three fit a stanza that ends in union with Siva.

1845.reading: Milk the milk that comes above the palate; milk the milk that oozes in the great egg; milk the milk that is not found in heaven; milk so that old torment ends.
1845.nuance: அண்ணாவின் மேல், above the palate, is exactly where khechari places the nectar, and பேரண்டம், the great egg, is the skull as cosmos in the Siddhars' body-as-egg doctrine; the two words make this the stanza where the cipher is nearest to plain. விண்ணாட்டில் இல்லாத sets this nectar above the gods' amrita.

1846.reading: Let the cattle that are the two deeds go, herdsman; pen the one cow that must be subdued, the mind.
1846.nuance: The herding songs (1846 to 1863) make each herd a numbered set of Saiva Siddhanta and the penning its mastery. Here the two deeds, good and bad, are released and only the mind is tied, which inverts the usual order: let karma run out, hold the mind.

1847.reading: The celibate ascetics beyond description reach the Supreme; those who spend every day as austerity come into the subtle presence.
1847.nuance: நைட்டிகர் are the lifelong celibates (naishthika), and தற்பரம், glossed as the Supreme, is the Vedantic word for the goal. சன்னம் is unclear: the subtle, or சந்நிதி, the presence; the stanza drops the herding image for a plain statement of who arrives.

1848.reading: Drive away the three cattle of egoity, herdsman; and daily subdue the cow called the states.
1848.nuance: Siddhanta counts three ahankaras (தைசதம், வைகாரிகம், பூதாதி) by the gunas, and the states (அவத்தை) are waking, dream and the rest; the verse treats both as herds that stray unless worked on daily (நாளும்).

1849.reading: Set apart and tie the cow called the one-mala being, herdsman; and drive off and tie the two malas that dwell in you.
1849.nuance: ஒருமலத்தன் is the soul with one mala, the விஞ்ஞானகலர் of Siddhanta who have only ஆணவம் left; the two malas of the herdsman himself are read as the other two, maya and karma. The pun on பசு (cow, bound soul) carries the stanza: the classes of souls are literally herds.

1850.reading: Twist and tie the cow called the three-mala being, herdsman; then you will know in advance all the truth of the three times.
1850.nuance: மும்மலத்தன் is the சகலர், the soul with all three malas, which is the human state; முக்கால நேர்மை, the truth of past, present and future, is a siddhi claimed as the fruit of penning it. முறுக்கி, twisting, suggests a harder beast than the one-mala cow of 1849.

1851.reading: Bind tight the three groups of senses, herdsman; and take up the flute of death and blow it, saying 'never'.
1851.nuance: இந்திரியத் திரயம் may be the senses of knowing, the organs of action and the inner instruments, or body, speech and mind. மரணக்குழல், the death-flute, blown to say என்றும் இல்லை, is either the flute that announces that death is no more or the flute that drives death off, as in 1844; the construction is loose.

1852.reading: Drive off the three goats called upadhi, herdsman; then all the deceit that is within you will run away.
1852.nuance: The three upadhis are the limiting adjuncts; tradition names the three bodies or the three kinds of affliction (தாபத்திரயம்). கள்ளம், deceit, is the inner falseness that depends on them; it goes by itself once they go.

1853.reading: Tie the cattle of the three bodies first, herdsman; after that there is no deceit, no ruin, and release is there.
1853.nuance: முக்காயம் are the gross, subtle and causal bodies of Vedanta and Siddhanta; முன்னம், first, gives the order of work. The stanza claims release as the direct fruit of penning the three.

1854.reading: Tie the cattle of the karma-mala at the end of the yard, herdsman; and tie the cow of the other karma-triad there too.
1854.nuance: கன்மமலம் is the second mala; the karma-triad is accumulated, ripening and fresh karma (சஞ்சிதம், பிராரத்தம், ஆகாமியம்). கடை is the end or edge of the pen, and perhaps 'last' in order, so karma is penned after the body and the ego.

1855.reading: Hobble the legs of the three causal cows, herdsman; and keep the practices firmly in hand.
1855.nuance: காரணக்கோ மூன்று may be the three causal bodies, the three causes of bondage (anava, karma, maya) or the three gunas as causes; the herding verb is hobbling, which fits a beast kept but not killed. சாதனங்கள், the practices, are endorsed here where 1818 dismissed them.

1856.reading: See the great light in the brahmarandhra, our herdsman; stay without speaking of release and reach great nishta.
1856.nuance: பிரம்மாந்திரம், the brahmarandhra, is the aperture at the crown, the top of the body-egg in Siddhar teaching, and the great light is seen there. முத்தி பேசாதிருந்து, not speaking of release, makes nishta a matter of silence, continuing 1831.

links.note: The Kural says the domain of the five must be crushed and all that one has wanted let go; Idaikkadar says those who let the senses loose like dogs are demons. Both make the restraint of the five the first condition, the Kural in the chapter on renunciation and the Siddhar in a herdsman's song.

The Kural says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is protection for seven; Idaikkadar says untied dogs are never fit for guarding. Both treat restraint of the senses as protection, the Kural from the side of the one restrained, the Siddhar from the side of what the senses are for.

Both use the snake asleep in its box. In the Sivavakkiyam the sleeping snake is the danger lust wakes, with the coiled power as the coded sense; in Idaikkadar the snake is the demon-mind charmed down into the box by the flute. The one verse warns against loosing the snake, the other shows how it is settled.

The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of saying 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'; Idaikkadar blows the flute so that neither 'mine' nor 'I' remains. The pair of words is the same; the Siddhar's means is to play the flute as the Lord's own.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will kindle the root fire in the hall of the moon and bring down the milk and drink it; Idaikkadar milks the milk that is in the head so as not to die. Both use milk for the nectar of the crown, Pattiragiriyar from the side of longing, Idaikkadar as a work-song for the yogi who has it.

Tirumular says that when the tongue-tip is pressed up into the middle, soul and Siva dwell there and the flesh does not die; Idaikkadar milks the milk that comes above the palate and oozes in the great egg so that torment ends. Both place the deathless nectar above the palate, and both claim an undying body from it.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will drive the wind-cow to the place and tie it; Idaikkadar tells the herdsman to pen the one cow that is the mind. The cow to be tied is the breath in the one and the mind in the other, and both poets make the herdsman's rope the figure for yoga.

Tirumular sets out the three classes of souls by their malas, those with two being the Rudras and the sakalas having three; Idaikkadar turns the classes into cattle, the one-mala being to be tied aside and the herdsman's own two malas driven off. The doctrine is Tirumular's and the herding is Idaikkadar's.

Tirumular says that for those who delight in the nada that shines at the crown there is no Yama; Idaikkadar tells the herdsman to see the great light in the brahmarandhra and sit in silent nishta. Both place the goal at the top of the head, Tirumular as sound and Idaikkadar as light.

source_issues: 1832 prints விட்டோ ர் with a space inside the word, the same ோ transcription artefact as in chapter 94.

1841 line 1 and 1842 line 1 lack the dash and the extra syllable (வெறு, மிக) that the other milking stanzas carry before the second refrain, so the metre of these two stanzas is short; no words seem lost.
1851 line 2: என்றும் இல்லை என்றே மரணக்குழல் எடுத்து ஊது is loosely constructed and may have lost a word.
